title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1, preregistration SHA-256 archived) to evaluate whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration relative to plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes and used 301 model calls. Observed outcomes: baseline = 299/300 valid (99.667%); guarded = 300/300 valid (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered planning assumption used for power calculations (planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed near‑ceiling baseline, removing statistical headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target. We report preregistered design choices, execution accounting, confirmatory statistics, a post‑hoc inferential sensitivity bound tied to the observed contingency counts, and artifact‑grounded recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations. All run artifacts and analysis outputs are archived in the execution manifest referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction: Translating operator intent into device configuration is a core NetOps operation. Large language models (LLMs) promise accelerated intent→configuration synthesis but introduce probabilistic failures—misordering, omission, and unsafe commands—that threaten operational safety. Prior work therefore recommends hybrid generate→verify→repair patterns combining probabilistic generators with deterministic validators and bounded repair loops to act as floor‑safety nets. Despite these proposals and lab demonstrations, rigorous preregistered evaluations that quantify how tightly bounded guarded pipelines change first‑pass misconfiguration rates under controlled sampling semantics remain scarce. We implement and preregister a narrowly scoped paired experiment to quantify the effect of a minimal guarded pipeline consisting of: (1) a single shared LLM candidate per task (single‑shot generation), (2) a frozen deterministic validator performing canonicalization and static dependency checks, and (3) at most one automated repair attempt when the validator reports violations. Our core research question: Can this minimal guarded pipeline reduce first‑pass misconfiguration rate relative to plain single‑shot generation under a controlled paired design? Contributions: (i) a preregistered paired experiment with deterministic seed generation and archived per‑task artifacts; (ii) confirmatory statistics derived from those artifacts; (iii) post‑hoc sensitivity tied to observed contingency counts; and (iv) artifact‑grounded recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations.
sections.related_work: LLM application to network configuration and intent translation has expanded rapidly. System demonstrations report promising intent→configuration synthesis in lab settings while documenting failure modes—misordering, omission, and overconfidence—that bear on operational safety [10.1002/nem.2313]. Adjacent domains (medical QA, code repair) show that verifier‑assisted and retrieval‑augmented pipelines reduce factual errors and improve grounding, motivating similar guarded architectures for NetOps [10.36227/techrxiv.176784505.56675782/v1, 10.2139/ssrn.6608518]. Deterministic network verification methods (e.g., header‑space analyses and specification checks) provide algorithmic foundations for validators that can statically check reachability and policy constraints without live execution [10.1145/3098822.3098834]. Survey and governance work emphasize auditability and human oversight as open challenges for production adopters [10.6028/nist.ai.100-2e2023]. Our study positions itself at the intersection of these strands by executing a preregistered paired evaluation that directly measures first‑pass validity under an explicit validator+repair floor‑guardrail.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and hypotheses: We preregistered the experiment (cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) and two confirmatory hypotheses: H1 — the guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus single‑shot generation; H2 — one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations. The preregistration included the planning assumption baseline pass rate = 0.40, which informed power calculations and target N. Design and sampling semantics: A paired within‑task design used a fixed deterministic seed list of 300 tasks. For each seed the same single LLM candidate (shared_initial_candidate) was used in both arms: the generator produced one configuration that served as the baseline and the starting point for guarded validation and possible repair. Planned episodes = 600; initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. This shared‑candidate design models operational workflows where a single proposed plan is reviewed and (if necessary) repaired; it increases within‑pair correlation and reduces expected discordant pairs relative to independent draws. Model and provider constraints: The declared generation model was gpt-5-mini and the execution contract limited total model calls to 600. The execution artifact model configuration records the model settings; specifically, execution/model_configuration.json records "temperature": null (sha256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). A null/unset temperature in the archived model configuration is not evidence of deterministic sampling (temperature=0); sampling determinism was therefore unspecified by the archived configuration and remains a potential source of generator variance that could affect cross‑draw heterogeneity. Validator and scoring semantics: The frozen deterministic validator canonicalized configurations to a normalized AST and applied static checks derived from the explicit workflow policies encoded in each task. The scoring rule was full intent‑constraint validation: success required satisfying the task's required_sequence, expected_final_state, and workflow policies. Validator traces record parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes, and a boolean valid flag; these structured traces triggered repair and recorded outcomes. Repair adapter: The preregistered repair adapter was invoked only when the validator reported violations on the shared candidate and was restricted to a single automated repair attempt. Repair inputs included the shared candidate and structured violation codes; repair outcomes were revalidated by the same deterministic validator. Contamination and exclusions: Exact normalized‑AST matching and prespecified near‑duplicate thresholds were used to detect contamination against preregistered artifacts; exact duplicates would trigger deterministic replacement from a reserve set. Primary estimand and analysis: The primary estimand was the absolute paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline). The preregistered primary test was the exact McNemar two‑sided test at α=0.05; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CIs (10,000 resamples, explicit seed) were preregistered. Secondary analyses and sensitivity treatments for failed provider calls were also specified.
sections.results: Execution accounting (artifact‑derived): Planned episodes = 600; completed episodes = 600; complete pairs analyzed = 300. Model calls used = 301 (300 shared initial generations + 1 repair invocation). No provider/infrastructure failures occurred per the preregistered retry policy; no deterministic contamination exclusions were required. Primary outcomes (archived counts): Baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); Guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). Archived paired contingency: n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Inferential results (preregistered): Exact McNemar two‑sided test p = 1.00. Observed absolute paired difference = 1/300 ≈ 0.0033333. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, bootstrap seed = 1729). Repair outcomes (H2): the single allowed automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1); Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]. Post‑hoc sensitivity bound: only one discordant pair was observed (n10 + n01 = 1), which imposes a hard upper bound on resolvable absolute paired difference of 1/300 ≈ 0.00333. Thus the preregistered target (≥50% relative reduction from planned baseline 0.40 → absolute ≈ 0.30) was infeasible given the observed near‑ceiling baseline; the archived contingency and bootstrap artifacts substantiate this arithmetic.
sections.discussion: Artifact‑grounded interpretation. The archived contingency (n11=299, n10=1, n01=0) directly constrains inferential outcomes: the absolute paired difference equals (n10 − n01)/N and the exact McNemar test conditions on the observed discordant count. With a single discordant pair the sampling distribution contains insufficient extreme outcomes to produce a small p‑value, explaining p = 1.00. The paired bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.01] expresses the same limitation: only extremely small absolute improvements are compatible with the data. Why preregistered planning assumptions matter. Our power plan assumed baseline = 0.40; the observed baseline (0.9967) collapses that expectation and removed statistical headroom. Designers should therefore calibrate task difficulty or adversarially augment tasks to produce a planned number of initial failures (or discordant pairs) aligned with the target effect size. Pairing semantics tradeoffs. The shared_initial_candidate design improves ecological validity for remediation workflows but reduces expected discordant counts and thus paired‑test power; independent draws address a different operational estimand and yield larger expected discordance for the same marginals. Repair effectiveness and sample‑size implications. H2 is a conditional estimand: 1/1 repair success yields extreme imprecision (wide Clopper–Pearson CI). To precisely estimate repair effectiveness designers must ensure a planned number of initial failures by adjusting task difficulty or augmenting the task bank. Construct validity and runtime semantics. Our validator performs static deterministic checks rather than dynamic emulation; runtime properties (control‑plane convergence, transient reachability) are therefore unmeasured. If operational claims require runtime guarantees, future studies should integrate emulation stages and preregister how emulator outcomes map to success/failure. Diagnostics and reproducible traces. The structured validator traces (normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, violation_codes, repair_applied) are essential for post‑hoc failure‑mode analysis and reproducible post‑mortems: they identify whether failures arise from missing commands, ordering violations, or preserved‑state violations. Operational implications. The run shows that a deterministic validator plus a bounded repair loop can correct some invalid candidates without human intervention, but the pipeline’s material effect in production depends on baseline error prevalence and validator coverage. Where baseline errors are rare, the validator is more valuable as a catastrophic‑risk mitigation floor than as a throughput amplifier.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=300 pairs) comparing single‑shot LLM generation (gpt-5-mini) to a guarded pipeline with a frozen deterministic validator and a single automated repair iteration. Baseline generation produced 299/300 valid outputs; the guarded pipeline produced 300/300 valid outputs. The single repair corrected the lone invalid baseline output, but the observed near‑ceiling baseline contradicted the preregistered planning assumption (baseline = 0.40) and removed statistical headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction. For future confirmatory NetOps evaluations we recommend: (a) calibrate task difficulty or adversarially augment tasks to ensure sufficient initial failures or target discordant counts; (b) preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets explicitly and incorporate them into power calculations; and (c) include emulation when runtime semantic claims are intended. All raw outputs, validator traces, repair traces, the execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived and enumerated in the Disclosure Statement to permit reproduction of the reported counts and intervals.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.
The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicts that assumption and removed headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.
Sampling semantics (shared_initial_candidate) reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference.

Validation used deterministic configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; actual runtime consequences of configurations were not executed and remain unmeasured.

H2 repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
